title: Representing Data: Histograms, Pie Charts and Broken-Line Graphs
seo_title: Grade 8 Representing Data Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Draw a variety of graphs by hand or technology to display and interpret data, including bar graphs and double bar graphs, histograms with given and own intervals, pie charts and broken-line graphs; critically read and interpret data represented in a variety of ways.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 8 worksheets: pie charts, histograms, broken-line graphs and interpreting data. 100 questions with memos.
key_sub: Only claim what the data shows.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Pie chart: sector angle = fraction × 360°.
  • A histogram shows grouped numerical data; the bars touch.
  • A broken-line graph shows change over time.
  • Check that a conclusion is really supported by the data.

Examples

Example

45 of 120 learners walk to school

45/120 × 360°

Answer: 135°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
100 for a pie chartUse 360°.
Reading the scaleCheck what each line is worth.
Unsupported claimsOnly say what the data shows.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 8 say about representing data?
faq.a: Draw and interpret bar graphs, double bar graphs, histograms, pie charts and broken-line graphs.

faq.q: When is a line graph best?
What is 90° in a pie chart?

faq.a: Yes, for example with a scale that does not start at 0.

The pie chart shows the choices of 40 learners. How many chose pasta?
All the angles at the centre of a circle graph add up to …
items.e: A circle graph is a whole circle, and a full turn is 360°. (100 is for percents.)

items.q: A sector is 25% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 25% × 360° = 0,25 × 360° = 90°. A sector of 25% is NOT 25°: it is one-quarter of the circle, a right angle.

items.q: A sector is 50% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 10% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 20% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 35% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 35% × 360° = 0,35 × 360° = 126°. (12,6° puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: A sector is 15% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 12,5% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 12,5% × 360° = 0,125 × 360° = 45°. Check: 12,5% is 18, and 360 ÷ 8 = 45.

items.q: A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 90°. What percent is it?
items.e: 90° ÷ 360° = 0,25 = 25%. (90% reads the degrees as a percent.)

items.q: A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 72°. What percent is it?
How many learners take the bus?
items.e: 25% = 14. 14 of 80 = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 learners. (25 is the percent, not the number of learners.)

items.q: How many learners ride a bike?
items.e: 10% of 80 = 80 ÷ 10 = 8 learners.

items.q: How many learners walk?
How many more learners walk than ride a bike?
items.e: Walk: 36. Bike: 8. 36 − 8 = 28 learners. (35 is the difference in percent, not in learners.)

items.q: How many learners chose granola bars?
items.e: 1% of 200 = 2. 35% = 35 × 2 = 70 learners. (35 would be right only for 100 learners.)

items.q: How many learners chose yogurt?
How many learners chose fruit or yogurt?
How many learners chose lacrosse?
items.e: 10% of 60 = 6 and 5% of 60 = 3. 15% = 6 + 3 = 9 learners. (4 comes from 60 ÷ 15.)

items.q: How many learners chose soccer?
items.e: 40% = 0,4. 0,4 × 60 = 24 learners. (2,4 puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: 24 of the 60 learners in a survey chose soccer. What percent is that?
items.e: 2460 = 25 = 0,4 = 40%. (36 is the number of learners who did not choose soccer.)

items.q: You have a table of counts. What do you do first to make a circle graph?
items.e: First add the counts to find the total. Then find each part as a percent of the total (or 360° ÷ total for each person).

items.q: To change a percent into a sector angle, you multiply the percent by …
A table shows that 9 of 36 learners chose basketball. What percent should the sector show?
items.e: 936 = 14 = 25%. (27 is the number of learners who did not choose basketball.)

items.q: 20 learners: walk 9, bus 6, car 5. Which sector angles are correct?
Walk 45%, bus 35%, car 20%. Which sector angles are correct?
items.e: Multiply each percent by 3,6°: 45 × 3,6 = 162°, 35 × 3,6 = 126°, 20 × 3,6 = 72°. They add up to 360°. (135°, 105°, 60° multiplies by 3, not 3,6.)

items.q: A table has a total of 50 learners. How many degrees stand for each learner?
items.e: 360° ÷ 50 = 7,2° for each learner. (2 uses 100 ÷ 50.)

items.q: A table shows that 7 of 40 learners chose the bus. What percent should the bus sector show?
items.e: 740 = 7 ÷ 40 = 0,175 = 17,5%. (28 multiplies 7 by 4 instead of 2,5.)

items.q: A table shows that 6 of 25 learners chose art. What angle should the art sector be?
items.e: Each learner is 360° ÷ 25 = 14,4°. 6 × 14,4° = 86,4°. (24 is the percent.)

items.q: Dumisani worked out the sector angles 150°, 120° and 80°. What is wrong?
items.e: 150 + 120 + 80 = 350. The angles of a circle graph must add up to 360°, so one angle is wrong.

items.q: What percent of the learners take the bus?
items.e: Read the label on the Bus sector: 25%.

items.q: How far had Ayanda biked after 15 minutes?
items.e: 15 minutes is halfway between 10 minutes (2 km) and 20 minutes (4 km). Halfway is 3 km.

items.q: How far had Ayanda biked after 5 minutes?
items.e: 5 minutes is halfway between 0 minutes (0 km) and 10 minutes (2 km). Halfway is 1 km. (5 is the number of minutes, not kilometres.)

items.q: How far had Ayanda biked after 25 minutes?
items.e: 25 minutes is halfway between 20 minutes (4 km) and 30 minutes (5 km). Halfway between 4 and 5 is 4,5 km.

items.q: How far had Ayanda biked after 35 minutes?
items.e: From 30 to 40 minutes the line is flat at 5 km. Ayanda was resting, so at 35 minutes she had still biked 5 km.

items.q: How far had Ayanda biked after 45 minutes?
items.e: 45 minutes is halfway between 40 minutes (5 km) and 50 minutes (7 km). Halfway is 6 km.

items.q: At about what time had Ayanda biked 8 km?
items.e: 8 km is halfway between 7 km (50 minutes) and 9 km (60 minutes). So it was at about 55 minutes.

items.q: Ayanda kept biking at the same speed for 10 more minutes after 60 minutes. About how far would she be then?
items.e: From 40 to 60 minutes she biked 2 km every 10 minutes. 9 km + 2 km = 11 km. Extending the line is only an estimate.

items.q: At about what time had Ayanda biked half of the 9 km?
items.e: Half of 9 km is 4,5 km. 4,5 km is halfway between 4 km (20 minutes) and 5 km (30 minutes), so about 25 minutes. (30 minutes is half the time, not half the distance.)

items.q: About how tall was the plant on day 10?
items.e: Day 10 is halfway between day 8 (12 cm) and day 12 (20 cm). Halfway between 12 and 20 is 16 cm. (10 is the day, not the height.)

items.q: About how tall was the plant on day 14?
items.e: Day 14 is halfway between day 12 (20 cm) and day 16 (26 cm). Halfway is 23 cm.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the height of a sunflower every week for 8 weeks?
c: Bar graph: it shows change over time
Line graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is measured again and again over time, so a line graph shows how it changes.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the favourite sport of the learners in your class?
c: Bar graph: it shows change over time
Line graph: it shows change over time
items.e: The data is in separate categories with nothing in between, so use a bar graph. Joining categories with a line makes no sense.

items.q: Ethan showed his class’s favourite sports with this line graph. What is wrong with it?
c: Sports are categories, so the dots should not be joined
The line should only go up
items.e: A line shows change from one point to the next, like over time. Sports have no order and nothing in between them, so Ethan should use a bar graph.

items.q: Goals scored by a ringette team in 5 games: 3, 5, 6, 8, 8. In a 6th game the team scores 0 goals. What is the new mean?
items.e: The total is still 3 + 5 + 6 + 8 + 8 + 0 = 30, but now there are 6 games: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 goals. (6 leaves out the 0, 30 is the total, and 5,5 is the new median.)

items.q: Goals scored by a ringette team in 5 games: 3, 5, 6, 8, 8. In a 6th game the team scores 0 goals. What is the new median?
items.e: In order: 0, 3, 5, 6, 8, 8. The two middle values are 5 and 6: (5 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5,5 goals. (6 is the old median, 5 is the new mean, and 7 uses 6 and 8.)

items.q: Goals scored by a ringette team in 5 games: 3, 5, 6, 8, 8. In a 6th game the team scores 0 goals. What is the new mode?
items.e: 8 still appears twice, and every other value appears once. Adding 0 does not change the mode.

items.q: A value greater than the mean is added to a data set. What happens to the mean?
items.e: The new value is above the mean, so it pulls the mean up. For example, the mean of 2, 4, 6 is 4; add 8 and it becomes 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

items.q: A value equal to the mean is added to a data set. What happens to the mean?
items.e: The new value is exactly at the mean, so it does not pull the mean either way. The mean of 2, 4, 6 is 4; add 4 and it is 16 ÷ 4 = 4.

items.q: Minutes 6 learners took to get to school: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 48. The 48 is removed. What is the new mean?
items.e: Without 48 the total is 12 + 14 + 15 + 15 + 16 = 72, and there are 5 values: 72 ÷ 5 = 14,4 minutes. (20 is the old mean, 12 divides by 6, and 15 is the median.)

items.q: Minutes 6 learners took to get to school: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 48. The 48 is removed. What happens to the median?
items.e: Before: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 48, so the median is (15 + 15) ÷ 2 = 15. After: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, so the median is the middle value, 15. It does not change.

items.q: Minutes 6 learners took to get to school: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 48. The 48 is removed. Which measure changed more when 48 was removed?
items.e: The mean went from 20 to 14,4. The median stayed at 15. An outlier like 48 pulls the mean a lot, but hardly moves the median.

items.q: A value is removed from a data set and the mean goes up. What was true about the removed value?
c: It was greater than the mean
It was equal to the mean
It was less than the mean
items.e: Taking away a small value removes something that was pulling the mean down, so the mean goes up.

items.q: Data: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 7. One 7 is removed. What is the new mode?
items.e: After removing one 7, the data are 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7. Now 3 and 7 each appear twice, so there are two modes.

items.q: How many more cans were collected in 2 026 than in 2 022?
items.e: 2 026: 2 750. 2 022: 2 500. 2 750 − 2 500 = 250 cans. (2 750 is the 2 026 total, and 100 is only the last year.)

items.q: By what percent did the number of cans grow from 2 022 to 2 026?
items.e: Growth = 250 cans. 250 ÷ 2 500 = 0,1 = 10%. (250% reads the cans as a percent, 25% divides by 1 000 instead of 2 500, and 100% would mean doubling: the steep line makes it look that way because the scale starts at 2 500.)

items.q: A poster says, “Our food drive more than doubled!” Is this supported?
items.e: Doubling 2 500 gives 5 000. The school collected 2 750, only 10% more. The scale starts at 2 500, so the line looks steeper than it is.

items.q: Which school has more learners who walk?
items.e: School A: 20% of 600 = 120. School B: 40% of 300 = 120. The Walk sector is twice as big at School B, but School B has half as many learners.

items.q: How many more learners take the bus at School A than at School B?
items.e: School A: 45% of 600 = 270. School B: 30% of 300 = 90. 270 − 90 = 180 learners. (15 is the difference in percent.)

items.q: In a random survey of 400 learners in a school board, 35% said they walk to school. The board has 18 000 learners. About how many of them walk?
items.e: Use the sample percent for the whole board: 35% of 18 000 = 0,35 × 18 000 = 6 300 learners. (140 is 35% of the 400 in the sample, and 11 700 are the ones who do not walk.)

items.q: A city has 750 000 adults. In a random survey of 1 500 of them, 42% said they skate in winter. About how many adults in the city skate?
items.e: 42% of 750 000 = 0,42 × 750 000 = 315 000 people. (630 is 42% of the sample, 31 500 has the place value wrong, and 435 000 are the other 58%.)

items.q: A bar graph’s scale is labelled 0, 10, 20, 100, 500, with equal spaces between the labels. Why is it misleading?
items.e: The space from 0 to 10 is the same as the space from 100 to 500, but one is 10 and the other is 400. Bars on this scale cannot be compared fairly.

items.q: An ad shows sales doubling with two loon pictures. The second loon is twice as wide and twice as tall. Why is this misleading?
c: It should be 3 times as tall
The big loon looks 4 times as big
items.e: Doubling both the width and the height makes the area 2 × 2 = 4 times as big. The eye sees the area, so sales look 4 times bigger instead of 2 times.

items.q: A newspaper circle graph of favourite summer activities says: camping 45%, swimming 35%, biking 30%. What is wrong?
items.e: 45 + 35 + 30 = 110. The sectors of a circle graph must add up to exactly 100%, so the graph cannot be right.
